flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
So, um, this is gonna get a little bit personal, but I did have a child who is having a rough time at home. So she came in crying, which is very unusual. And that's just something that is out of the ordinary for, you know, for this child, you know, because I always see her very happy, very jolly, and everything. And, you know, she was just nonstop crying and everything. So I was with a in the classroom with another one of my co workers. And, you know, I decided to take her outside, you know, because sometimes what could happen as well, even if something's going on at home, sometimes what could trigger those responses is usually, you know, being around a group of people, because, you know, some of these children, they're suffering from anxiety, depression, or sometimes undiagnosed anxiety or depression. So what I did was I took her outside, you know, just have her like, calm down, listen to the wind, you know, have her some touch some leaves and everything, because at the end of the day, sometimes it can just be very overwhelmed, maybe not at, not in the, like at the classroom or any other students, sometimes it's usually something that's just going on at home. So I sat down and asked her, you know, what's going on, she opened up to me about, you know, a situation that was going on in her household. And she just, we just started talking, you know, started talking, because I feel like sometimes these, these children, they just need a someone to talk to someone that actually cares, because maybe they don't actually receive it at home, or they don't receive it anywhere else. So sometimes they just need someone who cares, and is asking them, you know, like, how's your day been? How's, how's this going? How's school going? And everything.
